root.stem: A 64-year-old woman with years of aching, creaky knees, stiffness lasting under 30 minutes in the morning, and knee x-rays showing joint-space narrowing and bone spurs, felt a sudden pop behind her right knee while climbing stairs yesterday. Since then her right calf has become painful and swollen. A crescent-shaped bruise has appeared just below the inner ankle. For months before this she had noticed a soft, non-pulsatile fullness behind the knee that was most obvious when she stood with the knee straight. Imaging shows fully compressible deep veins and a fluid collection tracking from the back of the knee down into the calf.
root.oneliner: 64F + creaky knees + short morning stiffness + joint-space narrowing and bone spurs + sudden pop behind knee + painful swollen calf + crescent bruise below inner ankle + soft fullness behind knee, worse with knee straight + compressible deep veins + fluid tracking into calf
highlight: sudden pop behind her right knee
soft, non-pulsatile fullness behind the knee
most obvious when she stood with the knee straight
fluid collection tracking from the back of the knee down into the calf

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: A fluid-filled cyst behind the knee that has burst into the calf. The clincher: **a sudden pop behind an arthritic knee, then a swollen calf with a crescent-shaped bruise below the ankle bone and fully compressible deep veins**.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.note: Same lesion; named after the popliteal fossa behind the knee.

nodes.q: Between which two structures does the cyst usually form?
nodes.a: The medial head of the gastrocnemius and the semimembranosus tendon
nodes.note: It is a distended gastrocnemius-semimembranosus bursa that communicates with the knee joint.

nodes.q: How does fluid get into the cyst?
nodes.a: Excess knee joint fluid is pushed through a one-way, valve-like opening into the bursa
nodes.note: Fluid enters when the knee works but cannot easily flow back, so the cyst swells. That is why it is tense and most visible with the knee straight and softens when the knee bends.

nodes.q: Which underlying knee disease, shown by her x-rays, is making the extra joint fluid?
nodes.note: Any disease inside the knee joint can do it: osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, or a torn meniscus. In children the cyst is usually an isolated finding.

nodes.q: What causes the crescent-shaped bruise below her inner ankle?
nodes.a: Blood and joint fluid from the rupture tracking down between the tissue planes of the calf to below the medial malleolus
nodes.note: This is the crescent sign. It appears a day or more after the rupture.

nodes.q: Which serious complication can a large rupture cause in the calf?
nodes.note: Fluid under the deep fascia raises the pressure in the calf compartments. Watch for pain on passive stretch of the toes and tense calf compartments.

nodes.q: If her calf compartments become tense with pain on passive stretch of the toes, what is the treatment?
nodes.note: Untreated, rising compartment pressure cuts off the blood flow to the muscles and nerves, causing muscle necrosis and permanent nerve damage.

nodes.q: Which imaging test confirms the diagnosis and excludes a clot?
nodes.a: Ultrasound of the back of the knee and calf with compression ultrasound of the deep veins

nodes.q: What is the treatment?
nodes.a: Rest, ice, elevation and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, plus treatment of the knee disease (for example a corticosteroid injection into the knee)
nodes.note: Do not start anticoagulants: they are not needed and can worsen bleeding into the calf. Recurrent cysts are rarely removed surgically.

nodes.q: Her painful, swollen calf could suggest deep vein thrombosis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **A deep vein that does not compress on ultrasound**; risk factors such as recent surgery, immobility or cancer; no pop and no bruise below the ankle
**Sudden pop behind an arthritic knee + crescent bruise below the medial malleolus + fully compressible deep veins**

nodes.note: The trap: both give a painful, swollen calf, and a wrong label leads to needless anticoagulation. An intact large cyst can also press on the popliteal vein and cause a true clot, so the ultrasound must look at the veins.

nodes.q: Her sudden pop and calf pain could suggest a tear of the medial gastrocnemius. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **A pop in the middle of the calf while pushing off in sport**, with tenderness and a gap in the medial calf muscle on ultrasound
**A pop behind the knee in someone with knee arthritis + earlier fullness behind the knee + fluid tracking from the back of the knee**

nodes.q: The fullness behind her knee could suggest a popliteal artery aneurysm. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **A pulsatile mass** behind the knee, often in both legs and with an abdominal aortic aneurysm; it can clot and make the foot cold and pale
**A soft, non-pulsatile mass that is most obvious with the knee straight**

image_prompts.root: Soft pastel medical illustration of an older woman's right leg seen from behind and the side: a burst fluid-filled cyst in the hollow behind the knee leaking down into a swollen calf, and a crescent-shaped purple bruise curving just below the inner ankle bone; gentle colors, no text or labels.

root.stem: A 52-year-old woman who has had rheumatoid arthritis for 15 years notices that her right middle finger has slowly bent into a fixed position. The middle joint of the finger is bent and cannot be actively straightened, while the fingertip joint is bent backward. The middle joints of several fingers and the knuckles are swollen and warm, and the fingers at the knuckles drift toward the little-finger side. She can feel no cord or lump in her palm.
root.oneliner: 52F + rheumatoid arthritis 15 years + middle finger joint bent, cannot straighten + fingertip joint bent backward + swollen warm middle joints and knuckles + ulnar drift + no palm cord
highlight: middle joint of the finger is bent and cannot be actively straightened
no cord or lump in her palm

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: The clincher: **flexion of the proximal interphalangeal (PIP) joint with hyperextension of the distal interphalangeal (DIP) joint**.

nodes.q: Which part of the extensor tendon has failed?
nodes.a: The central slip, where it inserts on the base of the middle phalanx
nodes.note: The central slip is what straightens the PIP joint, so she cannot actively extend it.

nodes.q: Where do the lateral bands of the extensor mechanism slide, turning them into flexors of the PIP joint?
nodes.a: Toward the palm (volar to the axis of the PIP joint)
nodes.note: The head of the proximal phalanx pokes up through the gap like a button through a buttonhole (French: boutonnière). The tightened bands then pull the DIP joint into hyperextension.

nodes.q: Which nerve supplies the muscle whose tendon forms the central slip?
nodes.a: The radial nerve (its posterior interosseous branch)
nodes.note: The central slip is part of the extensor digitorum tendon. The interossei and lumbricals that feed the lateral bands are supplied mainly by the ulnar nerve.

nodes.q: In her, what has weakened the central slip?
nodes.a: Chronic synovitis of the PIP joint from rheumatoid arthritis
nodes.note: In people without arthritis the usual cause is trauma: a jammed finger forcing the PIP into flexion, or a cut over the back of the PIP joint.

nodes.q: Her knuckle swelling and drifting fingers come from synovitis at which joints?
nodes.note: Ulnar deviation at the metacarpophalangeal joints is another classic rheumatoid hand deformity. Rheumatoid arthritis spares the DIP joints.

nodes.q: In a fresh finger injury, which bedside test finds a central slip rupture before the deformity appears?
nodes.note: Bend the PIP joint 90 degrees over the edge of a table and ask the patient to extend the middle phalanx against resistance. A rigid, extending DIP joint means the central slip is torn.

nodes.q: How is an acute closed central slip injury treated?
nodes.a: A splint holding the PIP joint straight for about 6 weeks, leaving the DIP joint free to bend
nodes.note: Fixed deformities from long-standing rheumatoid arthritis may need surgery.

nodes.q: Her rheumatoid hand could also show swan neck deformity. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **PIP hyperextension with DIP flexion**
**PIP flexion with DIP hyperextension**

nodes.note: The trap: both are rheumatoid finger deformities, and they are mirror images of each other.

nodes.q: Her bent finger could suggest mallet finger. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **The fingertip droops in flexion and cannot be actively straightened; the PIP joint is normal** (terminal extensor tendon torn at the distal phalanx)
**The PIP joint is bent and the fingertip is bent backward** (central slip torn at the middle phalanx)

nodes.q: Her fixed bent finger could suggest Dupuytren contracture. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **A firm cord or nodules in the palm** pulling the knuckle and PIP joints into flexion, usually the ring finger; the DIP is not bent backward
**No palm cord; PIP flexion with DIP hyperextension**

root.stem: A 74-year-old man develops a hot, swollen, painful right knee 2 days after surgery to repair a hernia. His temperature is 37.9°C. He has diabetes, and his family says his skin has looked bronze for several years. Fluid drawn from the knee is cloudy with 25,000 white cells/µL, mostly neutrophils, and Gram stain shows no organisms. Under polarized light the fluid contains rhomboid-shaped, weakly positively birefringent crystals. An x-ray of the knee shows a thin line of calcium within the cartilage.
root.oneliner: 74M + hot swollen knee 2 days after surgery + 37.9°C + diabetes + bronze skin + 25,000 WBC, neutrophils, no organisms + rhomboid weakly positively birefringent crystals + calcium line in cartilage
highlight: thin line of calcium within the cartilage

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.a: Calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease, acute attack
nodes.note: The clincher: **rhomboid, weakly positively birefringent crystals** in the fluid of a hot knee.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.note: The name for the acute crystal arthritis of calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease.

nodes.q: Which crystal is in his joint fluid?
What colour are these crystals when lined up parallel to the axis of the red compensator?
nodes.note: Positive birefringence: blue when parallel, yellow when perpendicular. Urate crystals are the opposite.

nodes.q: What is the thin line of calcium in his cartilage called?
nodes.note: Classic sites: the menisci of the knee, the triangular cartilage of the wrist and the pubic symphysis.

nodes.q: Apart from any metabolic disease, which feature of his is the strongest risk factor for this disease?
nodes.note: Most patients are over 60. Onset before 60 should prompt a search for a metabolic cause.

nodes.q: Which event set off his attack?
nodes.note: Surgery, acute medical illness and joint trauma provoke attacks; so can a sudden fall in calcium after parathyroidectomy.

nodes.q: His bronze skin and diabetes point to which underlying disease that predisposes to calcium pyrophosphate deposition?
nodes.note: Other metabolic causes to screen for: hyperparathyroidism, hypomagnesemia and hypophosphatasia.

nodes.q: Which hand joints does the arthropathy of this underlying disease typically involve?
nodes.a: The second and third metacarpophalangeal joints
nodes.note: With hook-like osteophytes on x-ray.

nodes.q: Which cytokine, released after the crystals activate the NLRP3 inflammasome in macrophages, drives the attack?
nodes.note: It recruits the neutrophils that fill his joint fluid.

nodes.q: Which test is the first step for any hot, swollen joint?
nodes.a: Arthrocentesis with cell count, Gram stain, culture and crystal analysis
nodes.note: Crystals and infection can coexist, so the culture must come back negative.

nodes.q: What is the treatment of his attack once infection is excluded?
nodes.a: Aspiration and a corticosteroid injection into the knee
nodes.note: Alternatives: nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, colchicine or oral glucocorticoids. In an older man with diabetes, a joint injection avoids systemic side effects.

nodes.q: How does colchicine calm a crystal attack?
nodes.a: It binds tubulin and blocks microtubule polymerization, so neutrophils cannot migrate and degranulate
nodes.note: Low-dose colchicine is also used to prevent frequent attacks.

nodes.q: Why are urate-lowering drugs such as allopurinol of no use here?
nodes.a: The crystals are calcium pyrophosphate, not urate, and no drug dissolves them

nodes.q: Which chronic pattern can years of deposition produce?
nodes.a: A degenerative arthritis like osteoarthritis but in unusual joints (wrists, metacarpophalangeal joints, shoulders, elbows)
nodes.note: Called pseudo-osteoarthritis. Osteoarthritis in a joint it usually spares should make you think of calcium pyrophosphate deposition.

nodes.q: His hot knee could suggest gout. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Needle-shaped, negatively birefringent crystals** (yellow when parallel); classically the big toe
**Rhomboid, weakly positively birefringent crystals + chondrocalcinosis**; classically the knee

nodes.note: The trap: both are crystal arthritis set off by surgery or illness, and both respond to colchicine and anti-inflammatory drugs.

nodes.q: His low fever and 25,000 white cells could suggest septic arthritis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Organisms on Gram stain or a positive culture**, often more than 50,000 white cells/µL
**Crystals with a negative Gram stain and culture**

nodes.note: Crystals do not rule out infection; treat as septic until the culture is negative.

root.stem: A 34-year-old woman jammed her left ring finger catching a ball and now has pain and swelling at the base of the finger. She had noticed a painless bump there for years. An x-ray shows a well-defined lucent lesion inside the proximal phalanx with ring-and-arc calcifications, a thinned and slightly expanded cortex without periosteal reaction or soft-tissue mass, and a thin lucent line running across the lesion and its cortex without displacement.
root.oneliner: 34F + jammed ring finger + painless bump for years + well-defined lucent lesion inside proximal phalanx + ring-and-arc calcifications + thin cortex, no periosteal reaction + thin lucent line across lesion and cortex
highlight: well-defined lucent lesion inside the proximal phalanx
without periosteal reaction or soft-tissue mass
thin lucent line running across the lesion and its cortex

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: A benign cartilage tumor inside bone. The clincher: **a well-defined lucent lesion with ring-and-arc calcifications in a small bone of the hand**.

nodes.q: Which tissue makes up the tumor?
nodes.note: It arises from rests of growth-plate cartilage left behind in the bone.

nodes.q: In which part of the bone does it grow?
nodes.note: Enchondroma means cartilage inside the bone.

nodes.q: Which bones are its most common site?
nodes.a: The small tubular bones of the hand, especially the phalanges

nodes.q: What does the thin lucent line across the lesion after her minor jam represent?
nodes.a: A pathologic fracture through the tumor
nodes.note: The tumor thins the cortex, so a minor jam breaks it. Fracture is the usual way a hand enchondroma comes to attention.

nodes.q: Mutations in which enzyme genes are found in about half of solitary enchondromas and in most patients with many enchondromas?
nodes.note: The mutant enzymes make the oncometabolite 2-hydroxyglutarate. The mutations are somatic (mosaic), not inherited.

nodes.q: Many enchondromas in one patient, without vascular lesions, suggest which syndrome?
nodes.note: Many enchondromas plus soft-tissue hemangiomas is Maffucci syndrome. Both carry a high lifetime risk of chondrosarcoma.

nodes.q: Which malignant tumor can rarely arise from it?
nodes.note: Warning signs: new pain without a fracture, growth in an adult, cortical destruction, a soft-tissue mass, or a large lesion in the pelvis or upper femur.

nodes.q: How is her lesion managed?
nodes.a: Let the fracture heal, then curettage and bone grafting
nodes.note: An incidental, painless enchondroma is simply observed with follow-up x-rays.

nodes.q: A cartilage tumor in bone could be a low-grade chondrosarcoma. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Older adult, pelvis or upper femur, pain without fracture, deep scalloping or destruction of the cortex, soft-tissue mass**
**Small bone of the hand, painless until it fractures, well-defined with an intact cortex and no soft-tissue mass**

nodes.note: The trap: both are cartilage tumors with ring-and-arc calcifications.

nodes.q: Her bony bump could suggest an osteochondroma. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **A bony outgrowth from the surface with a cartilage cap, continuous with the medullary cavity**, usually near the knee, pointing away from the joint
**A lesion inside the medullary cavity** that expands the bone from within

image_prompts.root: Soft pastel medical illustration of a hand x-ray style view: the ring finger's proximal phalanx with a smooth oval clear area inside the bone containing small ring- and arc-shaped calcium flecks, thin bulging cortex and a fine crack across it; no text or labels.

root.stem: A 29-year-old man felt his lower back tighten while lifting boxes during a move yesterday. The pain is in the right lower back, does not travel down either leg, worsens with bending and twisting, and eases when he lies still. He has no morning stiffness. The muscles beside the lower spine are tender and in spasm; there is no tenderness over the spinous processes. Raising either straightened leg while he lies on his back causes no pain below the knee, and strength, sensation and reflexes in the legs are normal. He has no fever, weight loss or history of cancer, and no bladder or bowel problems or numbness around the groin.
root.oneliner: 29M + back tightened while lifting + pain stays in lower back + worse with bending, eases lying still + no morning stiffness + paraspinal tenderness and spasm + no midline tenderness + negative straight-leg raise + normal leg neuro + no red flags
highlight: does not travel down either leg
worsens with bending and twisting, and eases when he lies still
muscles beside the lower spine are tender and in spasm
no tenderness over the spinous processes
Raising either straightened leg while he lies on his back causes no pain below the knee
strength, sensation and reflexes in the legs are normal
no fever, weight loss or history of cancer
no bladder or bowel problems or numbness around the groin

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: The clincher: **back pain after lifting with tender, spasming muscles beside the spine, no pain down the leg and a normal neurologic exam**.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
Which tissue is injured?
nodes.a: The paraspinal (erector spinae) muscles and their tendons
nodes.note: Small tears from a sudden load cause pain and protective spasm.

nodes.q: Which branches of the spinal nerves supply these muscles?
nodes.note: The dorsal rami supply the deep back muscles and the skin over them; the ventral rami form the lumbar and sacral plexuses to the legs, which is why a strain spares the leg exam.

nodes.q: Raising his straightened leg while he lies flat causes no pain below the knee. Which test is this, arguing against a compressed lumbar nerve root?
nodes.note: A positive test reproduces pain shooting below the knee when the straight leg is raised between about 30 and 70 degrees.

nodes.q: What is the group of warning findings whose absence lets you skip imaging?
nodes.note: Fever, weight loss, history of cancer, bladder or bowel problems, saddle numbness, progressive leg weakness, major trauma, or injection drug use.

nodes.q: When is imaging warranted if no red flags are present?
nodes.a: Only if the pain persists beyond about 6 weeks of conservative care

nodes.q: What is the best initial management?
nodes.a: Stay active (no bed rest), heat, and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs
nodes.note: A short course of a muscle relaxant can be added if spasm limits sleep or movement.

nodes.q: Cyclobenzaprine, a common muscle relaxant, is structurally related to which drug class, explaining its sedating and anticholinergic effects?
nodes.note: It acts centrally in the brainstem rather than on the muscle itself. Avoid it in older adults.

nodes.q: What is the usual course?
nodes.a: Most patients recover within about 2 to 6 weeks

nodes.q: His pain after lifting could suggest a herniated lumbar disc. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Pain shooting below the knee in a dermatome + positive straight-leg raise**, sometimes with weakness or a lost reflex
**Pain stays in the back + negative straight-leg raise + normal leg neurologic exam**

nodes.note: The trap: both start with a lifting injury.

nodes.q: Back pain after lifting could hide cauda equina syndrome. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Saddle numbness + urinary retention or incontinence + weakness in both legs**; needs emergency magnetic resonance imaging and surgery
**No groin numbness, no bladder or bowel problems, normal leg strength and reflexes**

nodes.q: His sudden back pain could suggest a vertebral compression fracture. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Older patient with osteoporosis or on glucocorticoids, point tenderness over a spinous process**
**Young man, tenderness and spasm in the muscles beside the spine, none over the spinous processes**

nodes.q: Low back pain in a young man could suggest ankylosing spondylitis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Gradual onset over months, morning stiffness over 30 minutes, better with exercise and worse with rest**
**Sudden onset while lifting, worse with movement and better lying still, no morning stiffness**

root.stem: A 6-year-old boy has limped on his left leg for 2 months. On and off he complains of mild pain in his left knee and the front of his thigh, worse after playing. He has no fever and no recent illness, and he is short and thin for his age. Moving the left hip is painful and limited in some directions, and the left knee is normal on examination. His white cell count and erythrocyte sedimentation rate are normal. An x-ray of the pelvis shows a small, flattened, dense and fragmented left femoral head.
root.oneliner: 6M + 2-month limp + mild knee and thigh pain after play + afebrile + short and thin + painful limited hip motion + normal knee + normal labs + flattened dense fragmented femoral head
highlight: limped on his left leg for 2 months
mild pain in his left knee and the front of his thigh
no fever and no recent illness
short and thin for his age
white cell count and erythrocyte sedimentation rate are normal
flattened, dense and fragmented left femoral head
left hip is painful and limited

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: The clincher: **a chronic, mildly painful limp in a 4- to 8-year-old boy with a flattened, dense, fragmented femoral head on x-ray**.

nodes.q: What process damages the femoral head?
nodes.a: Idiopathic avascular necrosis (osteonecrosis) of the femoral head epiphysis

nodes.q: Which artery is the main blood supply of the femoral head at his age?
nodes.note: Its retinacular branches run up the femoral neck; the artery of the ligamentum teres adds little.

nodes.q: Why does he feel the pain in his knee when the knee is normal?
nodes.a: Pain referred from the hip along the obturator nerve
nodes.note: The obturator nerve supplies both the hip and the knee. A child with knee pain and a normal knee needs a hip exam.

nodes.q: Which two left-hip movements are most likely to be limited?
In a short, thin boy with this disease, what would a hand x-ray most likely show?
Which imaging is the first test?
nodes.a: Anteroposterior and frog-leg lateral x-rays of both hips
nodes.note: Early x-rays can be normal; magnetic resonance imaging then shows the necrosis. An early sign is a subchondral fracture line (crescent sign).

nodes.q: In what order does the femoral head change over time?
nodes.a: Sclerosis (dense), then fragmentation, then reossification, then remodeling
nodes.note: The whole process takes about 2 to 4 years. Both hips are involved in about 10 to 15% of children, usually at different stages.

nodes.q: Which factor best predicts a good outcome?
nodes.a: Younger age at onset (under about 6 years)
nodes.note: Younger children have more time to remodel the head. Collapse of the lateral part of the head predicts a worse outcome.

nodes.q: What is the treatment for him?
nodes.a: Observation, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and physical therapy to keep hip motion
nodes.note: Older children (over about 8) or those with severe head involvement may need surgery to keep the femoral head contained in the socket (osteotomy).

nodes.q: Which long-term joint disease follows a misshapen femoral head?
His limp and knee pain could suggest slipped capital femoral epiphysis (SCFE). How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Obese adolescent (about 10 to 16), the head slipped backward off the neck on x-ray, the hip rolls into external rotation when flexed**
**Age 4 to 8, short and thin, a flattened, dense, fragmented head that has not slipped**

nodes.note: The trap: both are painful limps with knee pain and limited internal rotation.

nodes.q: His limp could suggest transient synovitis of the hip. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Sudden limp after a viral illness, normal x-ray, gone within 1 to 2 weeks**
**Limp for months + flattened, fragmented femoral head on x-ray**

nodes.q: A painful hip in a child could be septic arthritis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Fever, refusal to bear weight, high white cell count and erythrocyte sedimentation rate**; an emergency
**No fever, normal labs, a chronic limp he can still walk on**

image_prompts.root: Soft pastel medical illustration of a small, thin, fully clothed 6-year-old boy limping on his left leg while pointing to his knee, with an inset pelvic x-ray showing the left femoral head flattened, dense and broken into fragments compared with a round right femoral head; no text or labels.

root.stem: A 17-year-old boy has found it harder to climb stairs and rise from low chairs over the past 2 years, and he now struggles to lift boxes onto a high shelf. His 20-year-old sister has the same weakness, and his parents, who are first cousins, are unaffected. To stand up from the floor he pushes his hands up along his thighs. His shoulder and hip muscles are weak and thin, while his face, eye movements and swallowing are normal, and he can whistle. His serum creatine kinase is 20 times the upper limit of normal. A muscle biopsy shows dystrophic changes without inflammatory cells, and staining for dystrophin is normal.
root.oneliner: 17M + 2 years of slowly worsening stair climbing and overhead lifting + affected sister, parents first cousins + pushes up along his thighs to stand + weak, thin shoulder and hip muscles + face, eyes and swallowing normal + creatine kinase 20x normal + dystrophic biopsy without inflammation + normal dystrophin
highlight: His 20-year-old sister has the same weakness
pushes his hands up along his thighs
shoulder and hip muscles are weak and thin
face, eye movements and swallowing are normal
20 times the upper limit of normal

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: An inherited muscle disease that wastes the shoulder-girdle and hip-girdle muscles. The clincher: **slowly progressive proximal weakness of shoulders and hips + very high creatine kinase + face spared + normal dystrophin**, in a family where a sister is affected too.

nodes.q: His parents are first cousins and his sister is affected. What is the most common inheritance pattern?
nodes.note: Most forms are recessive; a minority are autosomal dominant. Both sexes are affected, unlike the X-linked Duchenne and Becker dystrophies.

nodes.q: What is the name of the sign when he pushes his hands up along his thighs to stand?
nodes.note: It means weak hip and thigh extensors. It is not specific to Duchenne muscular dystrophy; any proximal myopathy can produce it.

nodes.q: Many forms come from faulty sarcoglycans. Which membrane complex, which anchors dystrophin and links the muscle cell to the surrounding matrix, do they belong to?
nodes.note: Other common culprits are calpain-3 (the most common form worldwide) and dysferlin (membrane repair). A leaky, fragile membrane lets creatine kinase escape and fibres die and are replaced by fat and fibrous tissue.

nodes.q: Which heart complication must be watched for in some forms?
nodes.note: Most frequent in the sarcoglycan and FKRP (fukutin-related protein) forms; it can end in heart failure or sudden arrhythmic death. Weakness of the breathing muscles is the other cause of death.

nodes.q: How do you screen for it?
nodes.a: Electrocardiography and echocardiography at diagnosis, repeated regularly
nodes.note: Check breathing with forced vital capacity at the same visits.

nodes.q: Which test confirms the diagnosis and its subtype?
nodes.a: Genetic testing with a muscular dystrophy gene panel
nodes.note: The biopsy with protein stains supports it; electromyography shows a myopathic pattern.

nodes.q: What is the treatment?
nodes.a: Supportive care: physical therapy and stretching, with cardiac and respiratory monitoring
nodes.note: No drug changes the course; steroids are not standard. Assistive devices and ventilation support are added as needed.

nodes.q: His proximal weakness and very high creatine kinase could suggest Becker muscular dystrophy. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **X-linked, so boys only (sisters are carriers) + reduced or abnormal dystrophin on biopsy**; calf pseudohypertrophy
**Normal dystrophin + an affected sister** (autosomal recessive)

nodes.note: The closest look-alike: same age, same proximal pattern, same high creatine kinase.

nodes.q: His proximal weakness could suggest polymyositis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Adult onset over weeks to months + inflammatory CD8 T cells in the muscle biopsy**; no family history; improves with steroids
**Slow course over years + affected sibling + dystrophic biopsy without inflammation**

nodes.q: His shoulder-girdle weakness could suggest facioscapulohumeral muscular dystrophy. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Facial weakness (cannot whistle or bury the eyelashes) + winged scapulae**; autosomal dominant
**Face spared (he can whistle)** with shoulder and hip weakness

root.stem: A 16-year-old girl who runs cross-country has had a dull ache around and behind both kneecaps for 3 months. It is worse going down stairs, squatting, and after sitting through a long film with her knees bent. There was no injury, and her knees never lock, give way or swell. Pressing the kneecap into its groove while she tightens her thigh reproduces the pain. When she does a single-leg squat, her knee drifts inward, and her hip abductors are weak. Her ligaments are stable, and there is no tenderness at the tibial tubercle, at the lower tip of the kneecap or along the joint lines. Knee X-rays are normal.

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: The most common cause of knee pain in active teenagers and young adults, especially girls. The clincher: **ache around and behind the kneecap that is worse on stairs, squatting and long sitting, with no injury and an otherwise normal knee exam**.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.note: Both names describe the same overuse syndrome. The older term chondromalacia patellae means softened cartilage under the kneecap and is not the same thing.

nodes.q: What is the name of the pain that comes on after sitting with the knees bent for a long time?
nodes.note: Long knee flexion keeps the kneecap pressed against the femur.

nodes.q: What is the bedside test that presses the kneecap into its groove while she tightens her thigh?
nodes.note: Pain on this test supports PFPS but is not very specific.

nodes.q: Which groove on the femur does the back of her kneecap press against?
nodes.note: Poor tracking of the kneecap from overuse, quadriceps imbalance and a wide Q angle concentrates the load on the cartilage under the patella.

nodes.q: Her knee drifts inward on a single-leg squat. Which weak hip muscle allows the femur to drop into this valgus position?
nodes.note: Weak hip abductors and external rotators let the femur adduct and rotate inward, pulling the kneecap off line.

nodes.q: Weakness of which part of the quadriceps lets the kneecap drift outward in its groove?
nodes.note: It is the only quadriceps part that pulls the patella medially; the lateral pull of the vastus lateralis and iliotibial band then wins. A wider Q angle (more common in women) adds to the lateral pull.

nodes.q: Which imaging does she need?
nodes.a: None; it is a clinical diagnosis
nodes.note: Image only for red flags such as trauma, effusion, locking, night pain or failure of treatment.

nodes.q: What is the treatment?
nodes.a: Exercise therapy that strengthens the quadriceps and hip muscles, with load reduction
nodes.note: Short courses of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), taping or foot orthoses may help; surgery is rarely needed.

nodes.q: Her age and running could suggest Osgood-Schlatter disease. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Tender, swollen tibial tubercle** from traction on the growth plate; jumping sports
**Ache around and behind the kneecap with no tibial tubercle tenderness**

nodes.note: Both are anterior knee pain in active teenagers.

nodes.q: Her anterior knee pain could suggest patellar tendinopathy (jumper's knee). How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Pain and tenderness at the lower tip of the kneecap**, worse with jumping
**Diffuse pain around the kneecap on stairs and long sitting, no point tenderness**

nodes.q: Her knee pain could suggest a meniscal tear. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Twisting injury + locking or catching + joint-line tenderness**, often with swelling
**No injury, no locking, no swelling, no joint-line tenderness**

His right second toe and left third finger are each swollen along their whole length like sausages, and the joints at the tips of several fingers are tender. He has silvery, scaly plaques on his elbows and scalp, and his fingernails have small pits and are lifting away from the nail bed. His heel hurts where the Achilles tendon inserts, and his lower back is stiff for an hour each morning. Serum uric acid is mildly raised. A hand X-ray shows erosions at the distal interphalangeal joints, a 'pencil-in-cup' deformity, and fluffy new bone at the joint margins, with no osteophytes.

joints at the tips of several fingers are tender
silvery, scaly plaques on his elbows and scalp
lifting away from the nail bed
lower back is stiff for an hour each morning

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: An inflammatory arthritis in people with psoriasis. The clincher: **psoriasis plaques with nail pitting + sausage digits + arthritis of the distal interphalangeal joints, with negative rheumatoid factor**.

nodes.q: Which group of joint diseases does it belong to?
nodes.note: Others: ankylosing spondylitis, reactive arthritis and arthritis of inflammatory bowel disease. Shared features: negative rheumatoid factor, enthesitis, dactylitis, spine and sacroiliac involvement, uveitis.

nodes.q: Which human leukocyte antigen (HLA) gene is linked to its spinal form?
nodes.note: A major histocompatibility complex (MHC) class I gene. The peripheral form is linked more loosely to HLA-B27; the skin disease itself is linked to HLA-C*06.

nodes.q: What is the name of the sausage-shaped swelling of a whole toe or finger?
nodes.note: Inflammation of the tendon sheaths and every joint of the digit at once; it also occurs in reactive arthritis.

nodes.q: What is the name of the inflammation where the Achilles tendon inserts on bone?
nodes.note: The enthesis (tendon or ligament insertion) is the primary target in spondyloarthritis.

nodes.q: What are the small depressions in his fingernails called?
nodes.note: With onycholysis (nail lifting), nail disease is found in most patients with psoriatic arthritis and predicts joint involvement.

nodes.q: The pencil-in-cup deformity is the hallmark of which severe, destructive form, with shortened, telescoping fingers?
nodes.note: Bone loss at the joint ends sits beside fluffy new bone formation, a mix not seen in rheumatoid arthritis.

nodes.q: Which cytokine axis drives both the skin and the joint disease?
nodes.note: Tumor necrosis factor alpha is also central, which is why both groups of biologics work.

nodes.q: Methotrexate does not help spine disease or enthesitis. Which drug class is usually started first for his back and Achilles disease?
nodes.a: A tumor necrosis factor (TNF) inhibitor, such as adalimumab
nodes.note: Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) for mild symptoms; methotrexate is the first disease-modifying drug for peripheral arthritis alone. Other biologics: interleukin-17 inhibitors (secukinumab, ixekizumab) and interleukin-12/23 or interleukin-23 inhibitors (ustekinumab, guselkumab). Apremilast and Janus kinase inhibitors are other options.

nodes.q: Before starting a tumor necrosis factor inhibitor, which infection must be screened for?
nodes.note: Use an interferon-gamma release assay or tuberculin skin test; blocking TNF breaks down the granulomas that wall off latent tuberculosis.

nodes.q: Which drug given by mouth is avoided because stopping it can flare psoriasis into pustular psoriasis?
nodes.note: Intra-articular injections into a single joint are acceptable.

nodes.q: His swollen finger joints could suggest rheumatoid arthritis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Symmetric metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints, sparing the distal ones + positive rheumatoid factor or anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide antibodies**; erosions with bone thinning, no new bone
**Distal interphalangeal joints + dactylitis + nail pitting, seronegative + pencil-in-cup with fluffy new bone**

nodes.note: The closest look-alike: both give erosive inflammatory arthritis of the hands.

nodes.q: His raised uric acid could suggest gout. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Sudden, very painful single joint (often the big toe) + needle-shaped, negatively birefringent crystals**; punched-out erosions with overhanging edges
**Months of several inflamed joints + psoriasis plaques + nail pitting**

nodes.note: Fast skin turnover in psoriasis raises uric acid, so the two can coexist.

nodes.q: His distal finger joints could suggest osteoarthritis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Hard bony nodes (Heberden nodes) + osteophytes and joint-space narrowing**; no dactylitis, no long morning stiffness
**Soft, inflamed joints + morning stiffness + erosions, no osteophytes**

It comes on after he walks two blocks or stands for a while and eases a few minutes after he sits down or bends forward; simply standing still does not help. He can walk much farther leaning on a shopping cart and can ride an exercise bike without pain. His foot pulses are strong and his ankle-brachial index is 1.1. Straight-leg raising is negative on both sides. Strength and reflexes are normal at rest, and he has no saddle numbness or bladder or bowel problems. X-rays show arthritis of the lumbar facet joints.

simply standing still does not help
ride an exercise bike without pain
no saddle numbness or bladder or bowel problems
arthritis of the lumbar facet joints

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: Narrowing of the lumbar spinal canal that squeezes the cauda equina roots. The clincher: **leg pain on walking or standing that is relieved by sitting or bending forward (shopping-cart sign), with normal pulses**.

nodes.q: What is the name of his walking symptom?
nodes.note: Called neurogenic because the nerve roots, not the leg muscles, run short of blood and space.

nodes.q: Why does bending forward relieve it?
nodes.a: Flexion enlarges the spinal canal and the nerve-root foramina
nodes.note: Extension (standing upright, walking downhill) narrows the canal; leaning on a cart or cycling keeps the spine flexed.

nodes.q: What is the most common cause?
nodes.a: Degenerative change: facet joint arthritis, a thickened ligamentum flavum and a bulging disc
nodes.note: Degenerative spondylolisthesis adds to it. It is a disease of people over 60.

nodes.q: Which imaging confirms it?
nodes.a: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the lumbar spine
nodes.note: Computed tomography myelography if MRI is contraindicated.

nodes.q: What is first-line treatment?
nodes.a: Conservative care: physical therapy with flexion exercises plus analgesics
nodes.note: Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) and weight loss; epidural steroid injections give short-term relief.

nodes.q: Which operation is used when conservative care fails or deficits progress?
nodes.note: Fusion is added if the spine is unstable (spondylolisthesis).

nodes.q: If the stenosis becomes severe, which emergency must you watch for?
nodes.note: Saddle numbness, urinary retention or incontinence and weakness in both legs. It needs urgent MRI and surgical decompression, or the bladder and leg loss can become permanent.

nodes.q: His leg pain on walking could suggest peripheral artery disease. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Calf pain relieved by simply standing still + weak pulses + ankle-brachial index below 0.9**; cycling hurts too
**Relief needs sitting or bending forward + strong pulses + normal ankle-brachial index**; cycling is comfortable

nodes.note: The classic trap: both are called claudication.

nodes.q: His leg symptoms could suggest a lumbar disc herniation. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Younger patient + sharp pain shooting down one leg below the knee + positive straight-leg raise**; worse sitting and bending forward
**Older patient + both legs + negative straight-leg raise + better sitting and bending forward**

root.stem: A 66-year-old woman has had 2 weeks of sharp mid-back pain that began after she lifted a bag of groceries. Menopause was at age 48 and she never took hormone therapy. She smokes a pack of cigarettes a day, weighs 50 kg, eats little dairy, and has taken prednisone every day for 6 years for polymyalgia rheumatica. Her mother broke a hip at age 70, and her sister had breast cancer. She is 4 cm shorter than at age 40 and the mid-thoracic spine is tender, with normal strength and sensation in the legs. Serum calcium, phosphate and alkaline phosphatase activity are normal, hemoglobin and creatinine are normal, and serum protein electrophoresis shows no abnormal band. A spine x-ray shows generalized loss of bone density and a wedge compression fracture of one vertebra.
root.oneliner: 66F + sudden mid-back pain after lifting + early menopause, no hormone therapy + smoker, 50 kg, low dairy + 6 years of prednisone + mother's hip fracture + sister with breast cancer + height loss + normal calcium, phosphate, alkaline phosphatase + no abnormal band on electrophoresis + wedge compression fracture
highlight: smokes a pack of cigarettes a day
Her mother broke a hip at age 70
Serum calcium, phosphate and alkaline phosphatase activity are normal

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: Too little bone, but the bone that is there is normal in composition. The clincher: **loss of bone density with a fragility fracture (vertebral compression after minor effort) and normal serum calcium, phosphate and alkaline phosphatase**.

nodes.q: Which blood pattern separates it from other bone-thinning diseases?
nodes.a: Normal serum calcium, phosphate and alkaline phosphatase activity
nodes.note: Bone is lost without a mineral or turnover signal in the blood. Raised alkaline phosphatase, abnormal calcium or an abnormal protein band points to another disease.

nodes.q: What does an iliac crest bone biopsy show?
nodes.note: Bone resorption exceeds bone formation, so there is less bone, not softer bone. Trabecular bone is lost first, which is why the vertebrae collapse.

nodes.q: After menopause, which cytokine, once called osteoclast-activating factor, rises in her bone?
nodes.note: Estrogen normally restrains interleukin-1, interleukin-6 and tumor necrosis factor. When estrogen falls they raise receptor activator of nuclear factor kappa-B ligand (RANKL) on osteoblasts, which binds RANK on osteoclast precursors and activates osteoclasts.

nodes.q: Loss of which hormone at her menopause lets bone resorption outpace formation?
nodes.note: Loss is fastest in the first 5 to 10 years after menopause. Early menopause, low body weight and never using hormone therapy add to the risk.

nodes.q: Which of her medicines speeds up the bone loss?
nodes.note: Glucocorticoids reduce osteoblast activity, increase osteoclast activity and lower intestinal calcium absorption. They are the most common drug cause of osteoporosis.

nodes.q: Which daily habit in her history, one she could stop, lowers bone density?
nodes.note: Other risks: heavy alcohol use, low body weight, malabsorption, immobility, and drugs such as anticonvulsants, proton pump inhibitors and heparin. Age and a parent's hip fracture are among the strongest fixed risks.

nodes.q: Which part of the history, needed in every osteoporosis risk assessment, revealed her low calcium intake?
nodes.a: Dietary history (calcium and vitamin D intake)
nodes.note: Peak bone mass is reached around age 30, and calcium, vitamin D and weight-bearing exercise build it. Her low dairy intake adds to the risk.

nodes.q: Why does a long stay on a space station or bed rest cause net bone loss?
nodes.a: Without weight-bearing load, bone resorption exceeds bone formation
nodes.note: Mechanical strain keeps osteoblasts active. Bodybuilding, anabolic steroids, a high-calcium diet and regular running do not cause net loss.

nodes.q: Which type of bone is lost first, so that her vertebrae collapse before her long bones break?
nodes.note: Vertebral bodies are mostly trabecular bone, so the vertebral compression fracture is the most common osteoporotic fracture. It can follow lifting or coughing, and repeated wedge fractures of the thoracic and lumbar spine cause loss of height and a stooped back (kyphosis). The distal radius and the hip are the other classic sites.

nodes.q: Which fracture carries the highest risk of death?
nodes.note: Surgery is needed, and immobility afterwards is what kills.

nodes.q: Which clot-related complication of immobility after a hip fracture can kill suddenly?
nodes.a: Pulmonary embolism from deep vein thrombosis
nodes.note: Pneumonia is the other common cause of death after hip fracture. Up to about 1 in 5 older patients die within a year.

nodes.q: Which test screens for it?
nodes.a: Dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry (DEXA) of the hip and spine
nodes.note: Screen all women from age 65, and younger postmenopausal women with risk factors. A fragility fracture of the spine or hip makes the diagnosis even when the T-score is better than -2.5.

nodes.q: Which T-score defines osteoporosis on DEXA?
nodes.note: The T-score compares her bone density with a healthy young adult, in standard deviations. Between -1.0 and -2.5 is osteopenia.

nodes.q: Which drug class is first-line treatment?
nodes.a: Bisphosphonates (such as alendronate), with calcium and vitamin D
nodes.note: Stop smoking, add weight-bearing exercise, and review the prednisone dose.

nodes.q: How do bisphosphonates raise bone density?
nodes.a: They bind bone mineral, are taken up by osteoclasts and trigger osteoclast apoptosis, so bone resorption falls
nodes.note: They are pyrophosphate analogs that bind hydroxyapatite. Alendronate is taken fasting with a full glass of water and sitting upright, to avoid pill esophagitis. Rare effects: osteonecrosis of the jaw and atypical femur fracture.

nodes.q: Her sister had breast cancer. Which selective estrogen receptor modulator protects her bone while blocking estrogen in the breast and the uterus?
nodes.note: It acts like estrogen on bone and blocks estrogen in breast and endometrium, and it lowers the risk of invasive breast cancer. It raises the risk of venous thromboembolism and can worsen hot flashes. Tamoxifen blocks the breast but stimulates the endometrium (endometrial hyperplasia and cancer).

nodes.q: Which monoclonal antibody lowers bone resorption by binding RANKL?
nodes.note: It stops RANKL from activating osteoclasts. Bone loss rebounds quickly if it is stopped.

nodes.q: Which drug builds new bone when it is injected once a day?
nodes.note: Intermittent parathyroid hormone stimulates osteoblasts more than osteoclasts, so bone formation rises; continuously high parathyroid hormone does the opposite. Avoided in Paget disease and after bone radiation because of an osteosarcoma risk.

nodes.q: Her back pain and compression fracture could suggest multiple myeloma. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Monoclonal spike on serum protein electrophoresis + anemia + high calcium or creatinine + punched-out lytic lesions**; usually normal alkaline phosphatase
**Normal protein electrophoresis, calcium and creatinine + diffuse loss of density**

nodes.note: The trap: both cause vertebral compression fractures with a normal alkaline phosphatase.

nodes.q: Her bone loss could suggest osteomalacia. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Low calcium or phosphate, high alkaline phosphatase, Looser zones, defective mineralization on biopsy**
**Normal calcium, phosphate and alkaline phosphatase; normally mineralized, thin trabeculae**

nodes.q: Her x-ray could show Paget disease of bone. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Thickened cortex, increased mineralization, high alkaline phosphatase**; enlarged, deformed bones
**Thin cortex and thin trabeculae, normal alkaline phosphatase**

nodes.q: With a sister who had breast cancer, her spine could hold metastases. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Focal lytic or sclerotic vertebral lesions, often with high alkaline phosphatase or high calcium**
**Diffuse loss of density with no focal mass and normal alkaline phosphatase and calcium**

nodes.q: Back pain with abnormal vertebrae could suggest ankylosing spondylitis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: Young man, **morning stiffness that improves with exercise, sacroiliitis, bamboo spine**
Older woman, **pain after lifting with a wedge compression fracture and lost height**

root.stem: A 13-year-old boy has had 4 weeks of aching pain in the left knee and thigh that got worse after he jumped off a school bus step this morning. He is at the 97th percentile for body mass index, and the skin of his neck folds is dark and velvety. He limps. His left knee examination is normal. When the left hip is flexed it rolls outward, and internal rotation of the hip is limited and painful. He has no fever.

highlight: internal rotation of the hip is limited and painful
4 weeks of aching pain in the left knee and thigh

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: The femoral head slips off the neck of the bone at the growth plate. The clincher: **an obese young adolescent with hip or knee pain, a limp, and a hip that rolls outward on flexion with limited internal rotation**.

nodes.q: Why does a hip problem cause his knee and thigh pain?
nodes.a: The pain is referred through the obturator nerve, which supplies both the hip and the knee
nodes.note: Always examine the hip in a child with knee pain; a normal knee examination is the hint.

nodes.q: Which way does the femoral head move?
nodes.a: It slips backward and downward relative to the femoral neck, through the growth plate
nodes.note: A Salter-Harris type I injury (the physis separates); the femoral neck moves up and forward while the head stays in the socket. It occurs during the adolescent growth spurt, ages 10 to 16, and is commoner in boys.

nodes.q: Which feature in his history is the main risk factor?
nodes.note: The dark, velvety neck skin (acanthosis nigricans) shows insulin resistance. Hypothyroidism, growth hormone treatment and renal osteodystrophy also raise the risk; a family history can too. Steroids raise the risk of avascular necrosis rather than of the slip.

nodes.q: Which imaging confirms it?
nodes.a: Anteroposterior and frog-leg lateral hip x-rays
nodes.note: The head sits behind and below the neck, like ice cream slipping off a cone; a line along the top of the neck no longer touches the head.

nodes.q: Which complication of an unstable slip is most feared?
nodes.a: Avascular necrosis of the femoral head
nodes.note: The blood supply to the head runs along the neck and tears when the head slips.

nodes.q: What follows years later in the damaged hip?
What is the treatment?
nodes.a: Stop weight-bearing at once, then pin the head in place with a screw (in situ pinning)
nodes.note: Do not attempt forceful reduction, which raises the risk of avascular necrosis. About 1 in 4 children slip on both sides, so the opposite hip is watched or pinned.

nodes.q: His knee pain after a jump could suggest Osgood-Schlatter disease. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: Adolescent athlete with **tender swelling of the tibial tubercle below the knee**; the hip examination is normal
**Knee examination normal; limited internal rotation of the hip with outward rolling on flexion + obesity**

nodes.note: The trap: both cause activity-related knee pain in a growing boy.

nodes.q: His limp and hip pain could suggest septic arthritis. How do you tell them apart?

**No fever, weeks of pain, can still walk with a limp; normal inflammatory markers**

nodes.q: A limp with hip pain in a boy could suggest Legg-Calve-Perthes disease. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: Age 4 to 8, **small, thin boy with a painless limp; avascular necrosis of the femoral head with a flattened, dense head on x-ray**

nodes.q: Pain referred toward the thigh in a teenage boy could suggest ankylosing spondylitis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Morning stiffness of the low back and buttocks that eases with exercise + sacroiliitis**; gradual onset
**Obese, activity-related hip and knee pain with limited hip internal rotation**

root.stem: A 10-year-old boy is brought in after his dentist found many unerupted and extra teeth, with baby teeth that have not fallen out. He is short, with a large forehead and widely spaced eyes, and his mother says he can touch his shoulders together in front of his chest. His intelligence is normal. highlight: baby teeth that have not fallen out
large forehead and widely spaced eyes
touch his shoulders together in front of his chest
His father has a similar appearance
wide-open sutures and many small extra skull bones

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: A defect of bones that form directly from membrane. The clincher: **absent or underdeveloped clavicles that let the shoulders meet in front of the chest + open skull sutures with extra small skull bones + extra unerupted teeth**. Exam words: frontal bossing, hypertelorism, Wormian bones, supernumerary teeth.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.note: Both names describe the same disease.

nodes.q: Which gene is mutated?
nodes.a: RUNX2 (runt-related transcription factor 2, also called CBFA1, core-binding factor alpha 1)
nodes.note: Many cases are new mutations.

nodes.q: How is it inherited, as his father's appearance suggests?
Which cell type does the RUNX2 mutation directly affect?
nodes.note: RUNX2 is the master transcription factor that turns mesenchymal cells into osteoblasts. Weak osteoblast function explains the low alkaline phosphatase activity in this case.

nodes.q: Which type of ossification builds the bones hit hardest?
nodes.a: Intramembranous ossification (clavicles and flat skull bones)
nodes.note: The sutures and fontanelles stay open, and small extra skull bones (Wormian bones) form between them. Long bones form mainly by endochondral ossification and are less affected.

nodes.q: Which long-term specialist treatment does he need most?

nodes.note: Intelligence is normal and life span is normal.

nodes.q: His bones could suggest osteogenesis imperfecta. How do you tell them apart?

nodes.q: His short stature and large head could suggest achondroplasia. How do you tell them apart?

root.stem: A 72-year-old woman has had 6 months of diffuse bone and muscle pain that gets worse with activity. She rarely goes outdoors, covers her skin when she does, and drinks little milk. She struggles to rise from a chair and walks with a waddling gait. Both shins are tender when pressed. Serum calcium is at the low end of normal, phosphate is low, parathyroid hormone is high, alkaline phosphatase activity is high, and 25-hydroxyvitamin D is low.
root.oneliner: 72F + 6 months of diffuse bone and muscle pain + rarely outdoors, covers skin, little milk + trouble rising from a chair, waddling gait + tender shins + low-normal calcium, low phosphate, high parathyroid hormone, high alkaline phosphatase, low 25-hydroxyvitamin D
highlight: struggles to rise from a chair

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: Soft bones from poor mineralization. The clincher: **diffuse bone pain + proximal muscle weakness + shin tenderness, with low-normal calcium, low phosphate, high parathyroid hormone and high alkaline phosphatase**.

nodes.q: What is wrong with the bone?
nodes.a: Newly formed osteoid does not mineralize
nodes.note: The bone matrix is made normally but stays soft, so bones bend and break easily. A biopsy shows excess unmineralized osteoid.

nodes.q: What is the same defect called in a growing child?
nodes.note: The growth plates are affected as well, causing bowed legs and beaded ribs.

nodes.q: What is the usual cause in her?
nodes.a: Vitamin D deficiency from little sun exposure and poor intake
nodes.note: Low vitamin D lowers calcium and phosphate absorption in the gut. Other causes: malabsorption, kidney or liver disease, and anticonvulsants.

nodes.q: Which hormonal response explains her high parathyroid hormone and low phosphate?
nodes.note: Low vitamin D lowers calcium absorption; parathyroid hormone rises, pulls calcium from bone and wastes phosphate in the urine. Busy bone-forming cells release alkaline phosphatase. Calcium stays near normal at the cost of the bone.

nodes.q: Which organ makes the active form of vitamin D, under the control of parathyroid hormone?
nodes.a: The kidney (1-alpha-hydroxylase in the proximal tubule)
nodes.note: The liver first makes 25-hydroxyvitamin D (the storage form measured to judge stores); the kidney then makes 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D (calcitriol).

nodes.q: Which x-ray sign is characteristic?
nodes.a: Looser zones (pseudofractures): thin lucent bands across the cortex
nodes.note: They sit on the inner femoral neck, pubic rami and ribs. Generalized loss of density is also seen.

nodes.q: What is the treatment?

nodes.q: Which three findings define it?
nodes.note: The enlarged spleen traps and destroys blood cells (hypersplenism). It is often found on examination or abdominal imaging.

nodes.q: Besides trapping in the spleen, what destroys her neutrophils?

nodes.q: Which infection-related event from her low neutrophil count can kill her?

nodes.note: The same type is linked to severe, seropositive rheumatoid arthritis.

nodes.q: What is the first step in treatment?

pink matrix, part of it calcified

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: The most common primary malignant bone tumor in children and adolescents. The clincher: **malignant cells that make osteoid (pink, partly calcified matrix) in the metaphysis around the knee of a child or teenager**.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.note: Both names describe the same tumor.

nodes.q: Where in the bone does it arise?
nodes.a: The metaphysis of a long bone near the knee (distal femur or proximal tibia)
nodes.note: The fast-growing end of the bone near the growth plate. It has a peak in adolescence and a smaller one in older adults with Paget disease or prior radiation.

nodes.q: What is the triangle of new bone where the tumor lifts the periosteum called?
nodes.note: The tumor lifts the periosteum, which lays down a triangle of new bone at its edge.

nodes.q: What is the pattern of new bone radiating outward from the tumor called?
nodes.note: Bone forms along vessels stretched outward from the cortex.

nodes.q: What do the tumor cells make?
nodes.a: Osteoid: malignant osteoblasts produce bone matrix
nodes.note: High alkaline phosphatase reflects the bone-forming cells.

nodes.q: Where does it spread first?
nodes.note: Blood spread is the rule for sarcomas; lymph node spread is rare. Lung metastases are the usual cause of death, so chest imaging is done at diagnosis and during follow-up.

nodes.q: Which inherited childhood eye cancer syndrome raises the risk of it later?
nodes.note: Li-Fraumeni syndrome (TP53 mutation), Paget disease of bone and prior radiation also raise the risk.

nodes.q: What is the treatment?
nodes.a: Chemotherapy before and after limb-sparing surgery
nodes.note: Regimens include high-dose methotrexate with leucovorin rescue, doxorubicin and cisplatin. Doxorubicin can cause cardiomyopathy and cisplatin can cause kidney and hearing damage.

nodes.q: His bone pain after a sports injury could suggest Ewing sarcoma. How do you tell them apart?

nodes.q: His bone destruction could suggest osteomyelitis. How do you tell them apart?

nodes.note: Wear and loss of joint cartilage. The clincher: **pain that worsens with use and eases with rest, stiffness under 30 minutes, and hard bony nodules at the finger joints, with a clear low-cell joint fluid**.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.note: Osteoarthrosis is also used. All describe the same wear-and-tear disease.

nodes.q: Which type of joint fluid does her knee aspirate show?
nodes.a: Non-inflammatory fluid: clear, yellow, under 2,000 white cells/mm3 with few neutrophils
nodes.note: **Clear fluid with few cells** separates it from inflammatory fluid (2,000 to 50,000 cells/mm3 in rheumatoid arthritis or crystal disease) and infected fluid (above 50,000).

nodes.q: What are the bony nodules at the end joints of her fingers called?
nodes.note: They sit at the distal interphalangeal (DIP) joints. Hard, usually painless bony swellings from osteophytes.

nodes.q: What are the bony nodules at the middle joint of her third finger called?
nodes.note: They sit at the proximal interphalangeal (PIP) joints. The metacarpophalangeal joints and wrists are usually spared.

nodes.q: What happens to her cartilage that makes the joint wear down?
nodes.a: Years of mechanical stress and ageing break down the cartilage matrix, so it loses its elasticity
nodes.note: Cartilage cells (chondrocytes) try to repair it but release destructive enzymes, and the bone underneath thickens.

nodes.q: Chondrocytes from osteoarthritic cartilage release more enzymes and inflammatory cytokines. Which product do they release less of?
nodes.note: They release more matrix metalloproteinases, interleukin-1 (IL-1) and tumor necrosis factor (TNF), while proteoglycan synthesis falls. Loss of proteoglycans makes the cartilage soft and lets it fissure.

nodes.q: What is the term for the dense bone under her worn cartilage on x-ray?
nodes.note: Her x-ray shows all four classic changes: joint space narrowing (cartilage loss), subchondral sclerosis, subchondral cysts and osteophytes (the bony spurs at the joint edge).

nodes.q: Besides age and weight, which kind of past event raises the risk in her left knee?
nodes.a: An earlier injury to the joint
nodes.note: Old joint trauma causes secondary osteoarthritis, as in a former boxer's wrist or footballer's knee. Obesity loads the knees and hips.

nodes.q: Given her antral ulcer, which analgesic is the safest first choice?
nodes.note: It relieves pain with almost no anti-inflammatory effect and does not irritate the stomach, so it is safe with an ulcer. Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) can worsen the ulcer. Weight loss and exercise go with it.

nodes.q: Why does low-dose ibuprofen give her only partial relief?
nodes.a: At low doses it works mainly as an analgesic; the anti-inflammatory dose is about twice as high
nodes.note: A larger dose would help the pain but would raise the risk of ulcer bleeding, which is why she needs a different plan.

nodes.q: Years later her knee is badly damaged and disabling despite drugs and joint injections. Which operation is offered?
nodes.note: Reserved for severe disease with disability. Intra-articular corticosteroid injection gives short-term relief before that.

nodes.q: Her hand swelling could suggest rheumatoid arthritis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Symmetric swelling of the metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints, warm and tender, morning stiffness over an hour**; spares the distal joints; inflammatory fluid
**Hard bony nodules at the distal and proximal finger joints, no warmth, stiffness under 30 minutes, worse with use**; clear fluid with few cells

nodes.note: The trap: both cause symmetric hand joint pain in middle-aged and older women.

nodes.q: Her knee swelling could suggest gout. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Sudden red, hot, exquisitely tender joint (often the big toe) with needle-shaped, negatively birefringent crystals** in the fluid
**Slow, mechanical pain over years, no flares, no crystals, no warmth** and clear fluid

nodes.q: Her knee could suggest pseudogout. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Acute swollen knee or wrist with rhomboid, positively birefringent crystals** and calcification of the cartilage on x-ray (chondrocalcinosis)
**No crystals and no cartilage calcification**, with slow pain that worsens with use

nodes.q: Her swollen knee could suggest septic arthritis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Fever, a hot red joint and fluid with more than 50,000 white cells/mm3**, mostly neutrophils
**No fever, no warmth, and clear fluid with 250 white cells/mm3**

nodes.q: Her knee and hand swelling could suggest Lyme disease. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Tick bite or expanding rash in an endemic area, then a hot swollen knee** weeks to months later; usually one or a few large joints
**No tick bite or rash, and bony nodules at the finger joints** with slow progression

nodes.q: The end-joint involvement of her fingers could suggest psoriatic arthritis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Psoriasis plaques or nail pitting, sausage-shaped fingers (dactylitis)**, inflammatory morning stiffness
**No skin or nail changes, hard nodules instead of soft swelling**, stiffness under 30 minutes

nodes.q: A friend says her joints are just ageing normally. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **No pain or loss of function**; cartilage water content falls but the joint space and bone stay normal
**Pain with use plus joint space narrowing, sclerosis and cysts on x-ray**; age is a risk factor, not the whole explanation

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: Excess, disorganised bone turnover in an older adult. The clincher: **a markedly raised alkaline phosphatase with normal calcium, phosphorus and parathyroid hormone, picture-frame vertebrae, and patchy focal bone-scan uptake**.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.note: Both names describe the same disease.

nodes.q: Which serum test is markedly raised, while calcium, phosphorus and parathyroid hormone stay normal?
nodes.note: ALP rises with osteoblast activity during rapid bone turnover. Normal calcium, phosphorus and parathyroid hormone (PTH) separate it from hyperparathyroidism and osteomalacia.

nodes.q: What does his normal gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT) tell you about the high ALP?
nodes.a: It comes from bone, not from the liver or bile ducts
nodes.note: GGT rises with liver and bile duct disease, so a normal GGT with normal liver enzymes points to bone.

nodes.q: What is the primary cellular abnormality?
nodes.a: Increased number and activity of osteoclasts
nodes.note: Osteoclasts resorb bone too fast (lytic phase), then osteoblasts lay down disorganised woven bone (mixed, then sclerotic phase) that is thick but weak.

nodes.q: What pattern does a biopsy of his pagetic bone show?
nodes.a: A mosaic pattern of woven bone with irregular cement lines
nodes.note: Also called a jigsaw-puzzle pattern; the marrow is replaced by loose, highly vascular fibrous tissue.

nodes.q: Which test shows how widespread the disease is?
nodes.note: It shows increased uptake in the affected bones (skull, spine, pelvis, femur). Radiographs show thickened cortex and picture-frame vertebrae.

nodes.q: Which type of fracture can his weak, bowed femur suffer after little trauma?
nodes.note: Pagetic bone is thick but weak, so long bones bow under weight and snap straight across the shaft.

nodes.q: What causes his hearing loss?
nodes.a: Overgrown skull bone narrows the foramina and compresses the vestibulocochlear nerve (cranial nerve VIII)
nodes.note: Involvement of the middle-ear ossicles adds a conductive component. The thickening skull also explains his growing hat size (cotton-wool appearance on x-ray).

nodes.q: Which heart complication can result from the very vascular pagetic bone?
nodes.note: The enlarged, highly vascular bone acts like a shunt, so the heart must pump more blood.

nodes.q: Which bone cancer is the feared late complication?
nodes.note: Suspect it when pain suddenly worsens or a mass appears in a long-standing pagetic bone, with a further rise in ALP.

nodes.q: Which drug class treats symptomatic disease?
nodes.note: They bind bone and inhibit osteoclasts. Calcitonin is a weaker alternative.

nodes.q: Which blood test is used to follow his response?
nodes.note: A fall toward normal shows disease control.

nodes.q: His back pain and dense spine could suggest bone metastases from prostate cancer. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Raised prostate-specific antigen** with patchy sclerotic deposits that do not enlarge the bone
**Normal prostate-specific antigen, picture-frame vertebrae, thick enlarged bone** and a very high ALP with normal calcium

nodes.note: The trap: an older man with back pain, sclerotic bone and a high ALP.

nodes.q: His bone pain could suggest osteoporosis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Normal ALP, calcium and phosphorus; low bone density**, fractures from thin bone
**High ALP and thick, dense, enlarged bone**

nodes.q: His bone pain could suggest osteomalacia. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Low or low-normal calcium and phosphorus with high PTH**, Looser zones, soft bones
**Normal calcium, phosphorus and PTH**, thickened bones

nodes.q: His high ALP could suggest primary hyperparathyroidism. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **High calcium with high or inappropriately normal PTH and low phosphorus**; subperiosteal resorption, brown tumours
**Normal calcium and PTH** with focal patchy sclerosis

nodes.q: His thick femoral cortex could suggest osteosarcoma. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: Teenagers, **metaphysis with sunburst pattern and Codman triangle**, destructive mass
Older adult, **uniformly thick, dense cortex over a long segment** without a destructive mass; osteosarcoma is only a late complication

nodes.q: His bone pain could suggest osteomyelitis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Fever, raised white cell count and erythrocyte sedimentation rate, focal bone destruction** and a periosteal reaction
**No fever; multiple dense bones on bone scan, very high ALP**

nodes.q: Which structures are the first target of the inflammation?

nodes.q: What does the spine look like on x-ray years later?

**Symmetric sacroiliitis in a young man with no skin or nail changes**

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?

An x-ray shows a thickened femoral shaft with erosion of the cortex from inside and scattered flecks of calcification. The resected mass is glistening, blue-gray and contains several cysts. Under the microscope, enlarged chondrocytes with irregular dark nuclei, some with two nuclei, lie within a cartilage matrix.

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: A malignant cartilage-forming tumor of adults. The clincher: **adult over 40 with constant deep pain, a thickened shaft with cortical erosion and stippled calcification, and atypical chondrocytes in cartilage matrix**.

nodes.q: Which tissue gives the resected mass its glistening blue-gray look?
nodes.note: The cysts come from myxoid change in the tumor.

nodes.q: Which microscopic feature marks it as malignant rather than a benign cartilage tumor?

nodes.note: Enchondroma cells look bland. Atypia plus invasion of bone mark malignancy.

nodes.q: Which bones are most often affected?

nodes.note: It peaks between ages 40 and 70. It arises in the medullary cavity, often from an enchondroma.

nodes.q: Which condition of many benign cartilage tumors inside the bones raises her risk?
nodes.note: Maffucci syndrome is multiple enchondromas plus soft-tissue hemangiomas, with an even higher risk. A solitary enchondroma or osteochondroma rarely turns malignant.

nodes.q: Which feature best predicts how it behaves?
nodes.note: Low-grade tumors rarely spread; high-grade tumors metastasise early.

nodes.q: Where does a high-grade tumor spread?
nodes.note: Local recurrence is also common after incomplete excision.

nodes.q: What is the treatment?
nodes.note: Chondrosarcoma responds poorly to chemotherapy and radiation, so complete resection is what cures it.

nodes.q: Her cartilaginous mass could suggest enchondroma. How do you tell them apart?

root.stem: A 38-year-old woman has had 4 months of pain and morning stiffness lasting about 90 minutes in both hands, and for the past year she has had trouble buttoning her blouse. Both wrists, the knuckles and the middle joints of her fingers are swollen, warm and tender, but the joints nearest her fingertips look normal. Her fingers drift toward the little-finger side at the knuckles, and several fingers bend backward at the middle joint and forward at the tip. Firm, painless lumps sit under the skin over both elbows. Hand x-rays show narrowed joint spaces and erosions at the edges of the middle finger joints. nodes.note: An autoimmune arthritis of the synovial lining. nodes.q: Which blood antibody is the most specific test for her disease?
nodes.note: More than 90% specific. Rheumatoid factor (IgM against the Fc part of IgG) is less specific: it is also raised in infections, other autoimmune diseases and some healthy people. Antinuclear antibodies can be positive too.

nodes.q: Which human leukocyte antigen (HLA) type is most strongly linked to her disease?
nodes.note: HLA-DR1 is also linked. Smoking adds risk by promoting citrullination of proteins.

nodes.q: If a biopsy of the swollen joint lining were taken, what would it show?
nodes.note: Thickened, inflamed synovium full of lymphocytes and plasma cells that grows over cartilage and erodes it and the bone. Necrotizing granulomas would suggest tuberculosis or granulomatosis with polyangiitis, a neutrophil-rich infiltrate would suggest infection, urate crystals mean gout, and pigmented villonodular synovitis is a benign hemosiderin-laden overgrowth.

nodes.q: Which cytokine released by activated macrophages is the main driver of this inflammation?
nodes.note: It activates synovial cells and osteoclasts, which destroy cartilage and bone.

nodes.q: Which other cytokine, also raised in the joint fluid, is blocked by the drug anakinra?
nodes.note: IL-1 and TNF-alpha together drive synovial inflammation and joint destruction. Anakinra is a recombinant IL-1 receptor antagonist, an option when TNF-alpha inhibitors fail or cannot be used.

nodes.q: Which white cell predominates in fluid aspirated from her actively inflamed knee?
nodes.note: An inflammatory fluid: usually 5,000 to 50,000 white cells per microliter, mostly neutrophils, with raised interleukin-1 and tumor necrosis factor-alpha, but no crystals and a negative culture.

nodes.q: Immune complexes form in her joint. What happens to the complement (C3) level in the joint fluid?
nodes.a: It falls, because the immune complexes consume complement
nodes.note: So the classic synovial fluid pattern is low C3, many neutrophils, and high interleukin-1 and tumor necrosis factor-alpha.

nodes.q: Which finger posture has she developed from tendon and ligament damage?
nodes.a: Swan-neck deformity (hyperextension of the proximal interphalangeal joint with flexion of the distal interphalangeal joint)
nodes.note: Boutonniere deformity is the reverse pattern (flexed middle joint, hyperextended tip).

nodes.q: What is the name of the drift of her fingers toward the little-finger side?
nodes.note: The fingers slip at the metacarpophalangeal joints as the inflamed capsule and ligaments stretch and the extensor tendons slide off the knuckles.

nodes.q: What would a biopsy of the firm lumps over her elbows show?
nodes.a: Central fibrinoid necrosis surrounded by palisading histiocytes (a rheumatoid nodule)
nodes.note: The most common extra-articular finding; seen mainly in rheumatoid factor-positive disease. Nodules can also form in the lungs.

nodes.q: Which syndrome combines her disease with multiple lung nodules in a coal miner or other worker exposed to mineral dust?
nodes.note: Rheumatoid nodules form in lungs damaged by coal dust, silica or asbestos. Interstitial lung disease and pleural effusion (low glucose) are other lung findings in her disease.

nodes.q: Before intubation for surgery, instability of which spinal joint must be considered?
nodes.note: Synovitis erodes the ligaments around the dens; neck extension during intubation can compress the spinal cord. Flexion-extension films of the neck before surgery.

nodes.q: Which iron-regulating hormone, raised in chronic inflammation, causes her anemia?
nodes.note: It blocks iron release from macrophages and gut absorption: anemia of chronic disease with low serum iron, low transferrin saturation and high ferritin.

nodes.q: Which rare complication of long-standing disease adds an enlarged spleen and a low neutrophil count?
nodes.note: Seropositive, long-standing disease with splenomegaly and neutropenia; recurrent infections are the danger.

nodes.q: Which drug is the first-line disease-modifying antirheumatic drug (DMARD)?
nodes.note: Give folic acid with it. DMARDs take 6 to 12 weeks to work. Watch for liver injury, bone marrow suppression, mouth ulcers and lung fibrosis; it is teratogenic.

nodes.q: Which enzyme does methotrexate inhibit?
nodes.note: Less tetrahydrofolate means less thymidine and purine synthesis. At the low doses used in her disease, the anti-inflammatory effect also comes from adenosine release. Leucovorin (folinic acid) bypasses the block.

nodes.q: Because DMARDs act slowly, which drug is given to control her symptoms until they work?
nodes.note: A low-dose, short-term glucocorticoid bridge. Hydroxychloroquine and auranofin are slow DMARDs; etanercept and infliximab are biologics and are also not quick.

nodes.q: If her disease stays active despite prednisone and methotrexate, which drug class is added next?
